newsitem.title: USA: TNP opens door to N.M. power deregulation.
newsitem.headline: TNP opens door to N.M. power deregulation.

text.p: Texas-New Mexico Power Co (TNP) said it is confident New Mexico will adopt its electricity deregulation plan, the first such plan proposed to offer customers a choice of power sellers in the state.

"We're the first utility in the state to file for deregulation," TNP spokeswoman June Norman said Wednesday, adding "we expect the NMPUC (New Mexico Public Utility Commission) to approve our community choice plan."
The plan to deregulate TNP's New Mexico power service, allowing customers to choose their electricity suppliers, goes before an NMPUC hearing on Feb 19.
Approval by the NMPUC is the final step needed to implement the plan.
No other New Mexico utilities have yet filed a deregulation plan with the NMPUC, Norman said.
TNP is one of four investor-owned utilities serving New Mexico.

TNP supplies power to over 218,000 customers, of which 43,000 are located in New Mexico. Its service territory includes 85 cities, nine of them in southern New Mexico, a few in north and west Texas, with the majority of the remainder in south Texas.

Under TNP's New Mexico deregulation proposal, customers would see a three-year transition to competition, during which customer rates, including fuel and purchased power costs, would be frozen at level equal to an average three percent reduction from December 1996 rates.
The transition period would likely begin several months after approval of the plan, the spokeswoman said.
Under the plan, customer aggregation would be determined by market forces, individual power suppliers could make proposals for service, and consumers would decide on options, TNP said.
TNP would also restructure its corporate organization so that its electricity transmission and distribution functions would be separated from its power supply operations.
During the transition period in the plan, purchased power savings and any other operational savings would be used to offset TNP's stranded costs in New Mexico, the company said.
Stranded costs are those costs incurred by the company, usually through large capital projects like power plant construction, which under a regulated environment are passed on to ratepayers.
Norman said TNP estimates it has stranded costs of $30-40 million in New Mexico.
The company's stranded costs in Texas are estimated at about $250 million, primarily due to the construction of the 300 megawatt TNP 1 power plant, which began service in 1990, Norman said.
TNP is a subsidiary of TNP Enterprises Inc, which is based in Fort Worth, Texas.
